- What Strata does NOT do (we do): no clock/governor capture ("no clock capture" is admitted in COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS L58), no formal A/A run, no ub=1 KL gating (its KL uses decode windows and a fixed config), no per-sample first-iteration-ramp exclusion.

Concrete rules for us to add:
1. Record `protocol_id` + corpus sha256 in every result; any change to prompts/caps/seeds/order = new id; `-text` gitattribute on fixtures.
2. Result schema: unavailable = null + pointer-keyed reason; status `complete|partial|nonconforming`; `n` kept honest.
3. Prompt-cache-reuse assertion (`cached_tokens` vs allowed shared prefix) on every serve-style run; restart between runs.
4. Report "capped / early-EOS" counts next to every decode rate; forbid pooling across context depths.
5. Adopt Strata's accept rule in `perf_summary`: median of per-round ratios >= +3% and > 2x A/A gap and > 2x drift, in all rounds (>=4 of 5 in confirm), plus <=2% regression on the other phase (pp when tuning tg).
6. Classify every optimisation as `exact` (byte-identical greedy output) / `numerically different` / `lossy`; only `exact` auto-accepted (our D027 "identical outputs" is that class).
7. Tag runs with the machine "noise state": record A/A gap and drift beside each A/B (we have A/A; make it a stored field).
8. Keep default vs custom tracks and a same-machine baseline for any claim.
9. Add a cell grid (prompt length x cached fraction x gen) and ABBA ordering for depth sweeps, which also addresses our Jetson first-sample clock-ramp artefact (J-E002).
10. For unified memory, adopt `memory_kind: shared` + the "pinned RAM costs 2x in a shared pool" kind of measured constant (`strata_control/uma_pool.py`: pool demand = fixed + cache slots x slot size + 2 x RAM-held experts; measured on 128 GB Strix Halo, hang with 41 s silent exit when overcommitted). Test whether our Jetson mmap/pinned path doubles residency (J-E003 saw +2.5 vs +1.8 GB cached).

## 3. Build / dependency management
- Python: `requirements.txt` exact pins with python_version markers and security-note comments (Pillow GHSA); `requirements-build.txt` (cmake, ninja pip wheels), `requirements-dev.txt`, `requirements-monitor.txt`; per-platform hashes-style lock files `packaging/locks/runtime-{linux-x86_64,linux-aarch64,darwin-arm64,windows-x86_64}-cp312.txt` produced by `packaging/lock_wheels.py`.
- Toolchain: `flake.nix` pins nixpkgs-unstable (flake.lock), CUDA 13.0 (`cudaPackages_13_0`) because 13.2.0/13.2.1 miscompile sm_120; x86_64-linux only; cmake/ninja from nix, not pip. `spark/build_engine.sh` warns on those toolkit versions. NOTE for us: CUDA 12.8/sm_120 is not the version they pin; their miscompile warning applies to 13.2.x, not 12.8, but check our toolkit before any 13.x move.
- CMake: `CMakePresets.json` v5 (new since ffa80d73): `cpu-check` (no GPU/no network), `cpu-check-native`, `cuda-compile` (`CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES "86-real;89-real;89-virtual"`), `hip-compile`; same flags as the release scripts so CI compile-only builds equal release builds. Vendored ggml (`third_party/strata-ggml`, `tools/check_vendored.py`) with `-DSTRATA_GGML_DIR` override.
- Docker: `Dockerfile`, `docker/` (entrypoint, healthcheck, smoke-test, compose per vendor), `.github/workflows/docker-images.yml`; the engine is fetched as a signed feed package (`packaging/feed_tool.py`, `signing.py`, `update_keys.json`), not built in the image.
- Packaging: per-platform build scripts, `package_engine.py`, signed feed with `min_driver`, `collect_libs.py`/`binary_deps.py` bundle CUDA libs.
- aarch64/Jetson/sm_87: aarch64 YES but only DGX Spark: `packaging/build_cuda_linux_aarch64.sh` + `spark/build_engine.sh` (default `ARCHS=121`, CUDA 13.0, glibc >= 2.39, driver >= 580.65, built on the device itself, "no older arm64 chroot"). `grep` for sm_87/Jetson/Orin in the repo (excluding third_party) finds no hit; sm_87 is not a target, CPU kernels for Q2_0/Gyro are x86-only. `CMakePresets` omit aarch64.
- Fit to our two targets: (a) reproducible pip-style pins + per-platform lock files are ADOPT for Python helpers (`cc/`, `lab/`); (b) CMake preset names `*-compile` = what our Build CC `cuda_compile_check` does, copy the "same flags as release" discipline; (c) nix flake is PATTERN only: x86 only and JetPack 6.2 cannot be nix-built (L4T driver stack), so for the Jetson keep host-native build + ccache; for amd64 CUDA 12.8 sm_120 a flake could pin nvcc/gcc, but our Docker/Buildx digest pinning already gives the same and works on both targets, so do not add nix; (d) record toolkit-version blacklist (miscompile warning) in the Build CC.

## 4. Code style / structure worth copying
- `AGENTS.md` (top-level agent contract: layout, install/launch commands, recommendation policy, links to AI_REFERENCE) plus `CONTRIBUTING.md` ("contributor responsible for every line", label unreproduced findings "unconfirmed static analysis", one problem per PR, do not resubmit declined proposals via another agent). ADOPT the evidence-labelling rule for our agent notes.
- `docs/README.md` rules: every guide has Title/Purpose/Quick start/Details/History; every measurement is preceded by a `**Measured on:**` line (hardware, model, version, workload); history in a final section, release notes or `history/` (finished campaigns moved with pointer files, `history/LINK-BASELINE.md` lists known-broken links). ADOPT the Measured-on line in our SUMMARY.md rows.
- One doc per mechanism (`KV_PREFETCH.md`, `DISJOINT_EXPERT_CACHE.md`, `BATCHED_DMA.md`, `VRAM_ELASTIC.md`, `NVFP4.md`) and contract docs: `docs/GDN_CONTRACT.md` ("audited on commit X; everything read from source; harness checks it against FP64 oracle", shapes table, tensor layout table, stage-name-to-timer table, note on misleading stage names). PORT the form for our moe_dispatch contract (shapes, layouts, which timer stage, oracle).
- Tests next to code layout: `tests/{core,cuda,gdn,tuning,snapshot,platform}`, `tools/test_*.py`, `serve/test_*.py`; CI split per concern in `.github/workflows`.
- Version-in-AGENTS.md and release-notes per version; `bench/results` indexed by `tools/bench_results_index.py --check`; capability table generated and checked (`tools/capability_table.py`, `docs/CAPABILITIES.md`).
- Gotcha to avoid: docs state hard counts (24,576 experts, 48 layers) in prose and code, which is why their tools are not reusable. Put shape constants in one config file.

## 5. Gaps neither project covers (goal: MoE ~4x device memory, unified memory + SSD, acceptable quality and t/s)
Strata does not either: its largest case (DeepSeek V4.1 2-bit) is 257 GB on a 128 GB Spark and still keeps experts in RAM/mmap plus CPU lane; the 4x oversubscription with SSD in the expert path is only touched via the n-gram table on SSD (NVFP4 locked-in-RAM measured 26 vs 39 tok/s decode). Gaps:
1. SSD expert streaming with prefetch/readahead and a cache hierarchy (VRAM/pinned/pagecache/SSD) on unified memory: no I/O model (queue depth, O_DIRECT vs mmap, NVMe bandwidth on Orin/Spark), no cold-start vs steady-state split. Strata has `tests/platform/direct_file_async.cpp`, `io_priority_test.cpp` and `serve/cache_drop.py` (page-cache give-back) only as small hooks.
2. Router-aware prefetch (predict next-layer experts from the current routing) and its accuracy measurement on traces; replay tools here only cover reactive eviction.
3. Quality under on-demand quantization/mixed precision and under expert skipping/substitution (Strata has `STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP`, KVA approximations, but no joint t/s vs KL Pareto per memory budget); our `cc/memory_pareto` is the nearest.
4. A trace corpus for a LARGE real MoE (routing skew at 256-512 experts, top-8+); we only have Granite 1B/400M-active (mild skew, D017). Strata's skew claims come from its own model.
5. Memory-limited execution test: hard enforcement of a device-memory cap on shared DRAM (our `gpu_budget` shim is untested on Jetson; Strata sizes from `MemAvailable - 6 GiB` heuristics, `DS4_UMA_HEADROOM_GIB`).
6. Thermal/clock/power state as a first-class covariate (neither records governor + clocks per sample; ours has nvpmodel/devfreq in summary but not per-sample).
7. Cost model that predicts t/s for (hit rate, miss cost, SSD bandwidth, overlap) validated end-to-end; our D019 says the overlap bound is not supported.
8. Crash/soak behaviour of a swap-heavy run (OOM killer / zram / page-cache thrash cliffs, our D015) with an automated guard that aborts before the host stalls.

2. PORT routing-trace policy simulators (replay_cache_policy.py, bench_eviction.py) with parameterised layers/experts.
3. ADOPT protocol hygiene: protocol ID + corpus sha + null-with-reason + cache-reuse assertion + nonconforming status.
4. ADOPT `tools/check_cuda_spills.py` in the Build CC gate; PORT quant_quality's top-64 renormalised KL/p99/segment set.
5. PATTERN: plan/apply/rollback with digest preconditions, launch-identity HMAC, GDN_CONTRACT-style contract doc.

# The interleaved small-batch matvec (STRATA_MMVQ_IL): how to measure a table for your card

The decode and verify windows run their dense projections (2 to 8 tokens at a time) through `native_mmvq_il`, which reads an
interleaved copy of the q8_1 activations. Every choice it makes gives the same bits as the plain kernels
(`STRATA_MMVQ_IL=0` turns the whole path off); only the speed differs. How many matrix rows one warp takes
(1, 2 or 4, or 0 = use the plain kernel) is a table in `src/kernels/cuda/native_mmvq.cu`, indexed by the
quantisation type (IQ4_XS, Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q3_K), the token count (2-4) and the matrix's row count (five classes).

## 1. Strata mechanism for models larger than memory

Strata is NOT a generic "stream everything from SSD" engine. It is a 3-tier expert placement: VRAM cache -> RAM (or mmap'd
file pages) -> SSD file tier. Hot experts are on GPU; misses are computed in place by CPU threads in parallel with the GPU.
- Resident on GPU: attention/DeltaNet mixers, routers, shared experts, head, KV (from 64K only its hot part, rest streams
  from RAM), plus an expert cache filling remaining VRAM (docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md:14-25).
- Resident in RAM: all experts, pinned; CPU computes the non-cached ones "in place" concurrently (HOW_IT_WORKS.md:27-29).
- Over-memory regime (the relevant one): DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw, 138 GB experts + 111 GB n-gram table. Experts go
  "as many as fit in graphics memory; the rest computed on the CPU, read in place from the model files"; n-gram table stays
  on SSD, a few rows per token (docs/DEEPSEEK41.md:13-17). "With less memory than that, part of the CPU's experts are read
  from the SSD while the model answers. It runs, slowly" (DEEPSEEK41.md:23-25). Measured: RTX5070 12GB + 64GB RAM + 3.6GB/s
  NVMe ~4.7 tok/s (DEEPSEEK41.md:63-65); Strix Halo 128GB unified, 109 GB experts in pool + 23 GB from SSD, 19-21 tok/s code
  (DEEPSEEK41.md:51-55). RAM-capped runs on 1 GPU: 26 tok/s unlimited -> 21/18/15/8 at 40/32/24/16 GB RAM (DEEPSEEK41.md:89-91).
  Planner: uma headroom = MemAvailable - 6 GiB (`DS4_UMA_HEADROOM_GIB`), because page cache of the model files is most of
  what cudaMemGetInfo counted (DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:84-86).
- Cache policy: ExpertCache::admit "never evicts" (include/strata/core/expert_cache.hpp:158-160); policy is instead an
  *adaptive tier* that swaps hot experts every N verify windows (`--adapt-every/--adapt-swaps/--adapt-decay`, up to 96 swaps,
  decayed heat counts; EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md:86-92; learned state saved as a profile, expert_cache.hpp:57-65). Optional per-layer
  slot ranges (expert_cache.hpp:171-190: global arrival-order filling measured 2.97% hit vs 21% for 8 slots/layer).
- Static plan = profile.bin: STRP header + (layer,expert) ranked by routing frequency + freq table (expert_cache.hpp:40-50);
  `--expert-profile` fills the cache in rank order at start. Shipped DeepSeek profiles `data/dsv41/profile-*.bin`
  (DEEPSEEK41.md:73-77); a profile for a different expert count is rejected by size (DEEPSEEK41.md:85-86).
- Prefetch/overlap: (a) lookahead predictor thread predicts next-layer misses from votes, scored as recall/precision
  (expert_source.cpp:3132-3200); (b) predicted experts are `pread` into staging on I/O threads (io_enqueue, newest-layer first,
  queue cap 512; expert_source.cpp:1249-1297) or `madvise(WILLNEED)` when mapped (expert_source.cpp:3036-3047); (c) a gate closes the
  read-ahead if <10% of bytes were used or the cache already holds the set (expert_source.cpp:2030-2060; probe every 256
  windows); (d) prompt path streams next layer's experts to GPU over PCIe during attention (HOW_IT_WORKS.md:51-53); (e) KV
  prefetch on a second stream, opt-in `STRATA_KV_PREFETCH=1`, only -4/-5% prefill (KV_PREFETCH.md:9-15,44-47).
- I/O path (Linux): O_DIRECT descriptors + kernel AIO (`io_submit`, 256 requests in flight per thread, 4 KiB-aligned,
  merged only where adjacent, 32 MiB merge cap; expert_source.cpp:2489-2492, 2868-2880). No io_uring found (grep). Or page-cache
  mmap with `POSIX_FADV_RANDOM` (expert_source.cpp:1185). It chooses at start with a probe: 8-thread O_DIRECT 1 MiB random
  preads vs 3-thread mapped first-touch, plus a "room" test on page cache vs cgroup limit (expert_source.cpp:796-801, 913-980;
  `STRATA_FILE_TIER_PROBE=0` disables). Staging buffers are pinned with `cudaHostAlloc` (1903-1914); complement arena
  `cudaHostAlloc(Mapped|Portable)` or paced `cudaHostRegister` (3854, 3962, 4005); THP via MADV_HUGEPAGE (src/core/pinned.cu:457-510);
  layer release by `MADV_DONTNEED` + `FADV_DONTNEED` (expert_source.cpp:4117-4123); `mlock` (src/platform/memory.cpp:167).
- Discrete-GPU-specific: exchange rotation (resident RAM complement <-> VRAM swaps, avoids a host memcpy; +10-15% decode,
  EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md:1-8,93-97), batched DMA (`cudaMemcpyBatchAsync`, CUDA>=13, PCIe; no demonstrated tok/s gain,
  BATCHED_DMA.md:1-7,59-63), disjoint expert slots across 2 GPUs (DISJOINT_EXPERT_CACHE.md:1-15), KV prefetch.
- Unified-memory-specific (DGX Spark): `--mmap-experts` = one copy, the file pages ARE the GPU cache (DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:40-42,
  70-71); UMA arena left unregistered on iGPU Radeon (include/strata/core/arch_defaults.hpp:50-55); don't mlock a table
  that competes with page cache (26 vs 39 tok/s, DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:81-82); Spark decode is GPU-launch bound (~930 kernels/token,
  DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:144-145) - same regime as our Orin finding.

## 2. Does Strata run on aarch64 + sm_87 + JetPack?

No, not as-is; plausibly not at all for our model sizes. Evidence:
- aarch64 is supported only on DGX Spark: "Nothing here is known to work on another ARM machine" (DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:3-6);
  needs CUDA 13.0 and driver 580.65+, glibc 2.39 (DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:25-26). spark/build_engine.sh:37-41 aborts unless nvcc
  is 13.x; JetPack here is CUDA 12.6. cmake/backends/cuda.cmake:23-25 default archs 86/89/120; arch >=75 accepted so sm_87 is
  not rejected by the arch check (cuda.cmake:55-61) but kernels were only tuned/measured on 86/89/120/121 (MMVQ_IL_TABLE.md:5-10).
- Build uses NEON ggml-cpu for CPU experts on aarch64 (CMakeLists.txt:72-73; src/kernels/cpu/portable.cpp:1); Q2_0/Gyro CPU
  kernels are x86-only (DGX_SPARK_LINUX.md:12-14). The CPU lane on 6 A78AE cores would be the bottleneck.
- Engine paths are model-hardcoded (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next geometry H=2560, FF=640 compile-time, expert_source.hpp:17-19; separate
  `src/qwen35` for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; `src/dsv41`). Supported list: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
  (MODELS.md:49-63, 267-290), all 12 GB+ NVIDIA RTX 30/40/50 (MODELS.md:68-75). Orin Nano 8 GB is far below the stated minimum
  (12 GB GPU + 46 GB RAM, MODELS.md:85-86).
- Portable/reusable: (1) algorithms: per-layer/global LFU-decay vs LRU vs Belady replay (tools/bench_eviction.py:1-30; GPU-free,
  runs on any `--dump-routing` trace); (2) profile format + builders (tools/make_profile.py:1-35, make_profile_mix.py: each trace
  normalised then weighted; note hard-coded `N_LAYER, N_EXPERT = 48, 512` at make_profile.py:~37, needs `--n-expert` and edit for
  40x256 or 48x128); (3) trace collection pattern (collect_profile_traces.py:1-17, 45-prompt corpus bench/profile_corpus.json);
  (4) the tier probe/gate heuristics as design; (5) tools/quant_formats.py (HTTP-range GGUF header reader). Tied to engine:
  cache slot banks, CPU expert pool, adaptive swap, io-prefetch, all CUDA kernels. MIT license allows lifting code.
- Trace format (make_profile.py:read_trace): repeating records `int32 layer, int32 k, k x int32 expert ids, k x float32 weights`.
  We can emit the same from a llama.cpp `cb_eval` hook on `ffn_moe_topk-%d` (common.h:498 has cb_eval) and reuse the tools.

## 3. llama.cpp 31288c9c6 oversubscription features

- `-lm/--load-mode auto|none|mmap|mlock|mmap+mlock|dio` (common/arg.cpp:2695-2709). **TRAP on Orin:** `auto` = mmap unless a
  device lacks `mmap_support` (src/llama-model.cpp:1590-1598); CUDA reports `mmap_support = type != IGPU`
  (ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:5498) and Orin is `prop.integrated` -> IGPU (cu:5472). So `auto` silently becomes "none"
  (read whole file into RAM) = OOM for a 20 GiB model. Must pass `-lm mmap` explicitly. `dio` (O_DIRECT, llama-model-loader.cpp:561)
  only changes how the load copies bytes; it does not make weights lazily paged, so it is not an oversubscription mode.
  `-lzm` lazy mode (only tensors >4 GiB, needs mmap) is for per-layer-embeddings, not experts (arg.cpp:2711-2722).
- `-ot/--override-tensor`, `-cmoe`, `-ncmoe N` (keeps experts of the FIRST N layers on CPU; arg.cpp:2758-2779). CPU-resident
  experts under mmap are page-cache pages computed by CPU threads.
- `--moe-cache-mib N` EXISTS (arg.cpp:2781-2789, env LLAMA_ARG_MOE_CACHE_MIB; src/llama-moe-cache.{h,cpp}): an LRU of the experts
  of host-resident MoE layers in device buffers ("moe_cache_lru", cpp:15-50). Per-layer slot map; the scheduler copy callback
  uploads only missing experts with `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async` (cpp:560-580), GPU computes everything (misses evict LRU
  head, cpp:72-114; layers with identical tensor layout share a bank group, cpp:167). Requires experts in host memory (`-ncmoe/-cmoe`);
  disables pipeline parallelism (llama-context.cpp:523). Warning if no layer is fully host (cpp:263). This is the closest
  analogue to Strata's GPU tier. Cost on UMA with pageableMemoryAccess=0: a real memcpy page-cache -> cudaMalloc bank, so
  cache MiB are DRAM taken from the 5.9 GiB budget (U: whether bank memory is counted by `--fit`).
- `--fit` default ON (common.h:483), margin 1024 MiB (common.h:488); ggml-cuda's UMA path reads MemAvailable (cu:5445-5450). It
  sizes -ngl/ctx, but with `-lm mmap` plus offloaded experts it cannot see page-cache pressure; set `-fit off` and size by hand
  for experiments. `llama-bench` has -ncmoe, -lm, -fitt but no moe-cache flag (llama-bench.cpp:474-480) -> use llama-cli /
  llama-server / llama-perplexity for cache runs.
- Fair default baseline (what an ordinary user would run): `llama-server|llama-cli -m M.gguf -lm mmap -ngl 99 -ncmoe <N>
  -c 4096 -fa on -fit off`, with N chosen so dense+KV+compute fit and remaining experts sit on CPU/mmap; also baseline B0 =
  `-ngl 0 -lm mmap` (pure CPU mmap). Always `-lm mmap`; never `none` for over-memory.

## 4. Proxy model recommendation

Usable memory 5.9 GiB. Target 14.8-26.6 GiB GGUF.
- **Primary: unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF, file `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`, 22.36 GB = 20.82 GiB = 3.5x** (HF tree API,
  sha not fetched). Arch `qwen35moe` (src/llama-arch.cpp:42 present at 31288c9c6). 40 layers (full attention every 4th, rest
  linear-attention/GDN), 256 experts, top-8 + shared expert, expert FFN 512, hidden 2048, 2 KV heads (HF config.json). Also
  Strata-supported (MODELS.md:267-290, Q4_K_XL is its listed 22.9 GB MTP variant). Pros: tiny KV (only 10 attention layers),
  expert = 2048x512x3 ~ 1.7-2 MB Q4 -> small, NVMe-friendly reads, ~3B active. Cons: GDN state; qwen35moe on sm_87 not yet
  validated here (U); experts are ~95% of bytes so dense part (~1 GiB) fits.
  Smaller siblings if memory-tight: UD-Q3_K_M 15.46 GiB (2.6x), UD-IQ4_XS 16.51 GiB (2.8x).
- Pure-llama.cpp-mature alternative: unsloth/Qwen3-30B-A3B-GGUF `Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf` 18.56 GB = 17.28 GiB = 2.9x; arch
  `qwen3moe` (arch.cpp:37), 48 layers, 128 experts, top-8, expert FFN 768, 4 KV heads (HF config). Not in Strata's list.
- **Fallback (~1.9x): ggml-org/gpt-oss-20b-GGUF `gpt-oss-20b-MXFP4.gguf` 11.28 GiB** (HF tree), arch `gpt-oss` (arch.cpp:131), 24
  layers, 32 experts, top-4, hidden 2880 (HF config). No requant noise, native MXFP4. Nearest ~1.5x options are
  worse fits: OLMoE-1B-7B Q8_0 6.85 GiB (1.16x, bartowski; 64 experts/16 layers, U) as a smoke test only.

## 5. First experiment plan (<=12 steps)

Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_XL (M); smoke/debug on gpt-oss-20b first. Use fixed prompt set (3 domains) and fixed seed.
1. Preflight: `swapon --show` (JetPack zram counts as memory; record or disable it for the run), `free -m`, record
   MemAvailable, `nvpmodel -q`, clocks fixed (`jetson_clocks`). Download M to NVMe; `fio`/`dd iflag=direct` sequential + 1 MiB
   random read MB/s (this is the ceiling: expect ~1-3 GB/s class; U).
2. Safety harness (every run): `systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=6200M -p MemorySwapMax=0` (or `ulimit -v` fallback) + a 1 s
   watchdog that SIGKILLs when MemAvailable < 350 MiB or PSI `memory some avg10` > 40; log `/proc/vmstat`
   (pgmajfault, pgpgin, pswpin/out), `/proc/meminfo` (Cached, Mapped, MemAvailable), `tegrastats`, `iostat -x 1`. Drop caches
   (`echo 3 > drop_caches`, needs root: confirm with user) before each cold run; also report warm run.
3. Reference for quality: (a) placement-invariance reference = same GGUF M on same box, `llama-perplexity -lm mmap -ngl 0
   --kl-divergence-base ref.kld` over ~10 chunks x 512 of wikitext + code + chat (slow, fine; logits file ~ n_vocab(248k)*4B*tokens
   -> keep tokens <= ~5k or use fewer chunks); (b) quant-vs-original reference = Q8_0 (34.4 GiB) via mmap from NVMe (cannot be
   resident; run once, hours) OR run the Q8_0 pass on a larger host and copy the .kld. Compare placements with
   `--kl-divergence` (expect KL~0, differences only CUDA vs CPU kernels).
4. B0 baseline: `-lm mmap -ngl 0` pure CPU mmap (page-cache bound). B1: `-lm mmap -ngl 99 -ncmoe 99(-cmoe)` GPU dense + all experts on
   CPU/mmap. B2: `-ngl 99 -ncmoe N` with N tuned to the minimum that avoids OOM (partial expert-GPU placement; GPU-layer experts
   count against DRAM). Record prefill (pp512, pp2048) and decode (tg128, tg512) t/s, cold + warm, major faults/token, NVMe MB/s.
5. C1: B1 + `--moe-cache-mib` sweep {256, 512, 1024, 1536} with `-fit off`; check DRAM high-water (cache + page cache + dense +
   KV). Expect page cache to shrink as banks grow; find the knee. Record cache hit rate if the stats log prints one (stats
   struct cpp:196-202).
6. Capture routing trace: patch-free `cb_eval` tool (new tool in our tree, not here) writing Strata-format records
   (`layer, k, ids, weights`) over decode of the 3 prompt domains; also record per-token sequences for replay.
7. Offline (no GPU) policy replay: `tools/bench_eviction.py` on the trace (adapt `--n-expert 256`, layers 40) at slot counts
   equal to the MiB sweep / expert bytes; compare fill-only, LRU, LFU-decay, Belady oracle, global vs `--per-layer`, and
   `--prefill` profile start. Gives the hit-rate headroom of `--moe-cache-mib` (LRU) vs a profile+LFU policy before writing code.
8. Profile pinning: `make_profile_mix.py` on traces of domains A/B -> ranked pairs; test on held-out domain C (transfer, as
   Strata did: 60% shipped vs 71% mixed, make_profile_mix.py:22-27). Implement as `-ot` regex lists pinning top-ranked layers'
   experts (granularity is whole layer tensor) or, better, a thin llama-moe-cache patch that pre-fills slots from profile.bin (C2).
9. C2/C3 (only if step 7 shows >10 points hit-rate gain): prefill-from-profile and LFU-decay in llama-moe-cache; re-run step 5 matrix.
10. I/O variants: `-lm mmap` default readahead vs `madvise(RANDOM)`/`posix_fadvise` set via an LD_PRELOAD shim or env patch;
    `MADV_WILLNEED` of next layer's selected experts (Strata mechanism). Measure major-fault stalls (perf trace -F / bpftrace
    `vmscan`), readahead_kb of the NVMe (`blockdev --getra`; test 0/128/2048 KiB).
11. Quality gate: KL/top-1 agreement vs step 3 ref for B0,B1,C1,C2 (should be equal within noise); report Δppl. Any lossy knob (expert
    top-k reduction as in Strata DeepSeek "Faster mode" 5 of 6, DEEPSEEK41.md:90) is a separate arm with its own KL.
12. Report per arm: decode t/s median of 3 (cold/warm), prefill t/s, majflt/s, NVMe MB/s average and p99 latency, DRAM
    high-water (MemAvailable min), cache hit rate, KL, any watchdog trips. Decision: if C1 decode >= 1.5x B1 at equal DRAM, adopt
    moe-cache; else consider profile-driven pinning. Abort any arm that trips the watchdog twice.

Caveats: GPU is Orin 1024-core, ~68 GB/s LPDDR5 shared with CPU; page-cache copies and bank memcpy compete for the same DRAM
bandwidth. Strata's Spark decode (~45 tok/s) shows the unified regime is launch-bound once experts are resident; our over-memory
regime will instead be NVMe-bound (active expert bytes/token ~ 8 experts x 40 layers x ~1.7 MB = ~0.5 GB/token worst case ->
at 2 GB/s ~4 tok/s upper bound with 0% cache hit; U, verify expert size from GGUF).

   struct cpp:196-202).

   (`layer, k, ids, weights`) over decode of the 3 prompt domains; also record per-token sequences for replay.
7. Offline (no GPU) policy replay: `tools/bench_eviction.py` on the trace (adapt `--n-expert 256`, layers 40) at slot counts
   equal to the MiB sweep / expert bytes; compare fill-only, LRU, LFU-decay, Belady oracle, global vs `--per-layer`, and
   `--prefill` profile start. Gives the hit-rate headroom of `--moe-cache-mib` (LRU) vs a profile+LFU policy before writing code.
8. Profile pinning: `make_profile_mix.py` on traces of domains A/B -> ranked pairs; test on held-out domain C (transfer, as
   Strata did: 60% shipped vs 71% mixed, make_profile_mix.py:22-27). Implement as `-ot` regex lists pinning top-ranked layers'
   experts (granularity is whole layer tensor) or, better, a thin llama-moe-cache patch that pre-fills slots from profile.bin (C2).
9. C2/C3 (only if step 7 shows >10 points hit-rate gain): prefill-from-profile and LFU-decay in llama-moe-cache; re-run step 5 matrix.
10. I/O variants: `-lm mmap` default readahead vs `madvise(RANDOM)`/`posix_fadvise` set via an LD_PRELOAD shim or env patch;

    `vmscan`), readahead_kb of the NVMe (`blockdev --getra`; test 0/128/2048 KiB).
11. Quality gate: KL/top-1 agreement vs step 3 ref for B0,B1,C1,C2 (should be equal within noise); report Δppl. Any lossy knob (expert
    top-k reduction as in Strata DeepSeek "Faster mode" 5 of 6, DEEPSEEK41.md:90) is a separate arm with its own KL.
12. Report per arm: decode t/s median of 3 (cold/warm), prefill t/s, majflt/s, NVMe MB/s average and p99 latency, DRAM
    high-water (MemAvailable min), cache hit rate, KL, any watchdog trips. Decision: if C1 decode >= 1.5x B1 at equal DRAM, adopt
    moe-cache; else consider profile-driven pinning. Abort any arm that trips the watchdog twice.

bandwidth. Strata's Spark decode (~45 tok/s) shows the unified regime is launch-bound once experts are resident; our over-memory
regime will instead be NVMe-bound (active expert bytes/token ~ 8 experts x 40 layers x ~1.7 MB = ~0.5 GB/token worst case ->

  on SSD, a few rows per token (docs/DEEPSEEK41.md:13-17). "With less memory than that, part of the CPU's experts are read

- Open: reproduce the early kills (order effects? page-cache charging of the bind-mounted binary? first container start?) — low priority.
EOF

| # | Guarantee | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Images bound to immutable id; same name cannot silently point at a different image | `lab image add` check |
| 2 | Idempotent submission by key; same key + different spec rejected; job.json write-protected | job-3d376c81fb dup/conflict |

| 10 | (HISTORICAL — lock removed in D007) GPU admission by flock serialised concurrent attempts (waited 3.5 s) | job C6-conc |

## Problems found (these drive the interface)
- P1 **Lock != exclusivity.** flock vanished with the dead runner while its container kept using the GPU (case 5). Admission must be tied to the *container's* lifetime / cgroup, or reconcile must precede re-admission.
- P2 **Recovery bug (D006):** first reconcile overwrote a finished result. Recovery must be phase-aware and results write-once. This was found only because the test killed the runner *in each phase*; "runner died" as one test would have missed it.
- P3 **No per-job single-active-attempt policy.** Two invocations of one job = two attempts (case 6). Needs an explicit policy (reject / queue / coalesce).
- P4 **Measurement confound is invisible to the lab:** SM clock at launch was 2955 MHz vs 1155 MHz across attempts; the lab records it but cannot control it. Perf tests need clock/warmup policy declared in the test, not guessed.
- P5 **First-rep warmup** in bench_pg samples (14.9k vs ~18k t/s): raw samples must be kept; averaging hides it.
- P6 **Root-owned outputs:** container ran as root, so converted GGUF is root-owned on the host. Cleanup/export needs a uid policy.
- P7 **Test definitions are code in the lab, not data.** Each new test (parser + assessor) required editing `bin/lab`. A test needs a declarative contract: command, input mounts, parser, assessor, whether it needs exclusive GPU.
- P8 **Wrapper blind spot (D001)** repeated at a larger scale: process-group tracking insufficient; label+token ownership worked.

=== decisions/D012-objective-memory-footprint.md
# D012 — Objective reframed: reduce GPU memory at similar accuracy and acceptable tokens/s (user, mid-session)
User: "our goal is to reduce memory usage on the GPU while having similar accuracy and acceptable tokens/s ... real challenge: super big MoE (500 GB weights into 128 GB memory + 4 TB SSD) ... target system is unified memory, we are discrete memory ... agent swarm; opus allowed for hairy tasks; codex for small tasks; may ask gpt6 astra via codex."
Consequences:
- Primary metric = GPU memory footprint (weights + KV + compute buffers; peak from nvidia-smi, cross-checked with llama.cpp's own buffer report); secondary = quality (paired KL / top-1 vs BF16, PPL) and decode/prefill t/s. Report a Pareto frontier, not a single "win". The earlier speed screens (D008-D011) are kept; speed-only candidate C1 (q8 activation reuse) is DEMOTED to a component/build-CC integration exercise.
- Scale analogy: 500 GB -> 128 GB is ~3.9:1. Granite BF16 = 2.67 GB => scaled GPU budget ~0.7 GB. Experiments report whether a configuration fits under the scaled budget. Labelled an ANALOGY, not full-scale evidence.
- Discrete vs unified memory: TRANSFERS: accuracy/KL, routing statistics, expert-usage skew, cache hit-rate-vs-capacity curves (trace replay), byte accounting, quantization effects. DOES NOT TRANSFER: PCIe copy cost/overlap, pinned-host staging, GPU-vs-CPU placement timing (on unified memory a "CPU expert" and a "GPU expert" share DRAM; the cost model is bandwidth contention + page residency vs SSD). Every result states which class it belongs to.
- SSD tier can be emulated campaign-locally (no host-wide cache flush): run with a container memory limit smaller than the mmap'd weights so page-cache eviction forces SSD re-reads.
- Method families to attempt (cheap screens first): representation (uniform + mixed per-tensor, experts lower-bit vs attention higher-bit), expert placement (--n-cpu-moe / -ot), KV cache quantization/context, trace-driven residency sizing (routing_trace + replay), SSD-tier emulation via cgroup memory limit. Strata-style adaptive slot caches are studied from source (map) and simulated via trace replay; llama.cpp has no adaptive expert cache.
=== decisions/D013-mixed-precision-frontier.md
# D013 — Representation Pareto for GPU memory (job-aa57700ee5; BF16 baseline logits artifacts/kl/bf16.kl, 20x512 wikitext-2)
Class: TRANSFERABLE (accuracy + byte accounting); t/s columns were taken with the engine build compiling in parallel => unscored.
- Experts are 90.4% of all weight bytes (Q8_0 GGUF: 1283.5 of 1420.5 MB) => the bulk-compression lever is expert precision; attention/embeddings (~10%) can stay high precision cheaply.
- Fixed overhead ~300 MiB GPU (CUDA context + KV + compute buffers; file size vs peak delta across variants) does NOT shrink with weights: scaled budget (0.26 x model) must be evaluated on weights+KV+buffers, and at this scale the floor is ~650 MiB of weights even at 2 bits.
- mixE4K vs uniform Q4_K_M at the same memory (1218 vs 1222 MiB): KLD 0.040 vs 0.078, top-1 90.5% vs 85.6%, PPL +2.9% vs +6.0%. Hypothesis (untested): Q4_K_M also quantizes attention tensors at 4-bit, which are small but sensitive.
- 3-bit experts: KLD 0.135 / top-1 81.8%; 2-bit experts collapse (KLD 0.77, PPL x2.09).
- Unanswered: sensitivity per layer/expert (routing flips under quantization noise), frequency-based per-expert precision (needs routing trace), imatrix-calibrated low-bit quantization (not tried; likely helps 3-bit), generation-level / task quality beyond wikitext KL.
=== decisions/D014-slot-cache-prediction.md
# D014 — Expert-granular slot cache: PREDICTION from real routing traces + measured static-offload calibration
Evidence: artifacts/traces/out/{prose,code,chat}.jsonl (Granite BF16, llama-routing-trace built via Build CC patch path, rt1: 18 s ccache build), experiments/routing/{prose,code,chat}.{json,md} (trace_replay), experiments/routing/predict_slots.py -> prediction.json; calibration job-36b7630119 (static --n-cpu-moe sweep, engine b0, mixE4K).
Observed (real): routing is skewed but only moderately: with 16 of 32 experts resident per layer, decode hit rate 70% (prose), 78.5% (code), 72% (chat) vs 50% for uniform; 24 slots: 88-94%. Code > prose > chat at 16 slots => domain-dependent (advice: do not generalise).

=== decisions/D015-ssd-tier-emulation.md
# D015 — SSD-tier emulation via container memory limit (job-6e6b2d39b8; engine b0, mixE4K, --n-cpu-moe 24, own-file cold cache)
Class: MIXED. Transfers: the existence/shape of the page-cache cliff, I/O accounting method, cold-vs-warm discipline. Does NOT transfer: absolute t/s (discrete GPU, Zen2 CPU AVX2, PCIe, local NVMe, Linux page cache; target is unified memory with its own SSD).
Method: all expert weights file-backed in host memory (GPU holds attention+embeddings only: 572-576 MiB), `docker --memory L --memory-swap L`, posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) on the model file only (no host-wide flush), cgroup memory.peak and io.stat rbytes sampled at 4 Hz.
Result (pp512 / tg64, 3 reps; CONCURRENT COMPILE LOAD avg ~18 on 16 threads => speeds are lower bounds): limit -> tg t/s, SSD read: 1536m -> 129, 1.6 GiB; 1024m -> 79, 4.1 GiB; 768m -> 15, 28.8 GiB; 640m -> 3, 95.7 GiB; 560m -> 1, 135 GiB. All runs exit 0, no OOM kill.
Interpretation: working set ~ process anon (~400 MiB incl. CUDA/ggml buffers) + ~750 MiB expert bytes. Once the limit drops below it, decode becomes SSD-bound with heavy read amplification (reads >> useful bytes: 135 GiB for a run of a few hundred tokens). Advisor bound tokens/s <= effective SSD B/s / fetched B/token is consistent with the ~15 t/s point if nearly every expert is re-fetched each token (~160 MiB/token if all 192 activations miss).
Implication for the target: naive mmap + OS LRU has no notion of routing skew or layer order; an explicit hot-expert residency policy + prefetch/read-ahead control is the component to evaluate (trace-driven sizing in D014 gives the hit rate that policy needs).
Caveat to fix in a clean rerun: CPU contention; 1 repetition per limit; the 1536m row includes the initial model load reads.
=== decisions/D016-image-identity-confusion.md
# D016 — Build CC recorded the wrong "image config id" (found by independent observation, T-K)
Evidence: experiments/handoff-real/verdict.json (first rejection), cc/engine_handoff/example-real/{facts.json,verdict.json}, archive builds/results/b0-baseline-3/engine-image.docker.tar (index.json top digest sha256:cf383f82..., manifest.json Config sha256:7c2b92ad...).
Finding: with Docker 29's containerd image store, `docker image inspect .Id` returns the OCI INDEX digest (cf383f82...), not the image config digest (7c2b92ad...). The Build CC (written by Codex T-D from the brief's own warning) still stored the inspect Id as the image identity; `lab image-load --expect-config-id` therefore "verified" a value that is not a config id. The handoff tool refused to admit it because it re-observed the archive instead of trusting the record. It also showed the record hashed 7 of 19 executables in /app (libraries omitted).
Why it matters: the brief says to distinguish archive hash, Docker config ID, platform manifest digest and index digest; a lab that loads the archive needs the identity that the receiving engine can actually check.
Fix: Build CC now records image.docker_reported_id, image.config_digest, image.index_digest, image.index_manifests (parsed from the saved archive) and app_files (all regular files in /app), with a note; unit test asserts they are separate. Admission (lab image-load) to use archive-derived ids (next).
Lesson (methodology + Manager): identity checks must be performed by an independent observer on the delivered bytes; a record written by the producer is a claim. Two CCs written independently agreed on field names but not on meaning.
=== decisions/D017-routing-skew-control.md
# D017 — Is Granite routing skew real? (answering claim-register P12; ProMoE says modern MoEs have near-uniform expert access)
Evidence: experiments/routing/{control_uniform,prose,code,chat}.json (trace_replay), artifacts/traces/out/*.jsonl. Control = SYNTHETIC uniform-random top-8 trace (24 layers x 2000 decode tokens), labelled.
- Control hit rate (LRU and LFU) = slots/32 exactly (12.4, 24.9, 37.4, 49.9, 74.9%): simulator has no bias.
- Real Granite decode traces (cold start, 96-160 decode tokens, single sequence): LRU at 8 slots prose 49% / code 36% / chat 45% (LFU up to 49%) vs 25% control; at 16 slots 70-81% vs 50%; at 24 slots 88-94% vs 75%. => within-request skew/temporal locality is REAL for Granite.
- Mild: normalised usage entropy 0.88-0.92 (1.0 = uniform). Pooling the three workloads raises it to 0.936; top-8 hottest experts overlap 0.47 between workloads (random 0.25). => partially shared hot set, weaker when pooled; consistent in direction with MoE-Infinity (skew within request, weaker pooled) and ProMoE (near-uniform at scale).
Limits: 3 workloads, 1 sequence each, 96-160 decode tokens (cold-start dominated), prefill excluded from decode stats, Granite != target. Does NOT show the target model's routing is skewed. Needed before sizing any hot-expert cache: target-model traces across domains, long decodes, pooled multi-request.
Effect on D014: the prediction stands only as "if the target routes like Granite"; it must be re-derived from target traces. Claim P12 status: partially supported locally for Granite (within-request), pooled-uniformity question open.

# D018 — Directive (user, mid-session): apply Strata's concepts to Granite to reduce GPU memory; impose a memory restriction to simulate a super-big MoE
Answer to "have you applied Strata stuff?": not before this point (only studied, ran 4 CPU tests; used llama.cpp-native quantization and static --n-cpu-moe). Now:
1. Memory restriction = GPU budget shim (T-L, cc/gpu_budget): hard cap + virtual cudaMemGetInfo, scaled budget ~700 MiB (500GB->128GB ratio x 2.67GB), plus the container cgroup limit for the host/SSD tier (D015).
2. Strata concept -> Granite: expert residency table with hot experts in fast memory and cold in host memory, expert-granular placement. Proposed mechanism for llama.cpp: expert tensors in CUDA managed memory (each expert is one contiguous byte range of the ggml tensor: offset e*nb[2]); per-layer hot sets from routing traces get cudaMemAdvise(PreferredLocation=device)+prefetch; cold experts stay host-resident and are read by the same kernels (maps onto unified memory); static hot sets need no host sync and keep CUDA graphs. Dynamic LRU slots (Strata's hit_hook) are a later step. Delegated to an Opus agent (hard systems task).
Honesty: managed-memory behavior under oversubscription on this driver/GPU is unverified; PCIe remote reads are discrete-only cost; result classes will be labelled.

- Primary metric = GPU memory footprint (weights + KV + compute buffers; peak from nvidia-smi, cross-checked with llama.cpp's own buffer report); secondary = quality (paired KL / top-1 vs BF16, PPL) and decode/prefill t/s. - Scale analogy: 500 GB -> 128 GB is ~3.9:1. Granite BF16 = 2.67 GB => scaled GPU budget ~0.7 GB. Experiments report whether a configuration fits under the scaled budget. Labelled an ANALOGY, not full-scale evidence.
- Discrete vs unified memory: TRANSFERS: accuracy/KL, routing statistics, expert-usage skew, cache hit-rate-vs-capacity curves (trace replay), byte accounting, quantization effects. DOES NOT TRANSFER: PCIe copy cost/overlap, pinned-host staging, GPU-vs-CPU placement timing (on unified memory a "CPU expert" and a "GPU expert" share DRAM; the cost model is bandwidth contention + page residency vs SSD). Every result states which class it belongs to.
- SSD tier can be emulated campaign-locally (no host-wide cache flush): run with a container memory limit smaller than the mmap'd weights so page-cache eviction forces SSD re-reads.
- Method families to attempt (cheap screens first): representation (uniform + mixed per-tensor, experts lower-bit vs attention higher-bit), expert placement (--n-cpu-moe / -ot), KV cache quantization/context, trace-driven residency sizing (routing_trace + replay), SSD-tier emulation via cgroup memory limit. Strata-style adaptive slot caches are studied from source (map) and simulated via trace replay; llama.cpp has no adaptive expert cache.
=== decisions/D013-mixed-precision-frontier.md
# D013 — Representation Pareto for GPU memory (job-aa57700ee5; BF16 baseline logits artifacts/kl/bf16.kl, 20x512 wikitext-2)
Class: TRANSFERABLE (accuracy + byte accounting); t/s columns were taken with the engine build compiling in parallel => unscored.
- Experts are 90.4% of all weight bytes (Q8_0 GGUF: 1283.5 of 1420.5 MB) => the bulk-compression lever is expert precision; attention/embeddings (~10%) can stay high precision cheaply.
- Fixed overhead ~300 MiB GPU (CUDA context + KV + compute buffers; file size vs peak delta across variants) does NOT shrink with weights: scaled budget (0.26 x model) must be evaluated on weights+KV+buffers, and at this scale the floor is ~650 MiB of weights even at 2 bits.
- mixE4K vs uniform Q4_K_M at the same memory (1218 vs 1222 MiB): KLD 0.040 vs 0.078, top-1 90.5% vs 85.6%, PPL +2.9% vs +6.0%. Hypothesis (untested): Q4_K_M also quantizes attention tensors at 4-bit, which are small but sensitive.
- 3-bit experts: KLD 0.135 / top-1 81.8%; 2-bit experts collapse (KLD 0.77, PPL x2.09).
- Unanswered: sensitivity per layer/expert (routing flips under quantization noise), frequency-based per-expert precision (needs routing trace), imatrix-calibrated low-bit quantization (not tried; likely helps 3-bit), generation-level / task quality beyond wikitext KL.
=== decisions/D014-slot-cache-prediction.md
# D014 — Expert-granular slot cache: PREDICTION from real routing traces + measured static-offload calibration
Evidence: artifacts/traces/out/{prose,code,chat}.jsonl (Granite BF16, llama-routing-trace built via Build CC patch path, rt1: 18 s ccache build), experiments/routing/{prose,code,chat}.{json,md} (trace_replay), experiments/routing/predict_slots.py -> prediction.json; calibration job-36b7630119 (static --n-cpu-moe sweep, engine b0, mixE4K).
Observed (real): routing is skewed but only moderately: with 16 of 32 experts resident per layer, decode hit rate 70% (prose), 78.5% (code), 72% (chat) vs 50% for uniform; 24 slots: 88-94%. Code > prose > chat at 16 slots => domain-dependent (advice: do not generalise).
Measured static layer offload (discrete GPU, PCIe-dependent => DISCRETE-ONLY): mixE4K GPU MiB / decode t/s: n0 1218/704, n6 1056/336, n12 894/212, n18 734/161, n24 576/128. Memory falls ~27 MiB per layer moved; speed falls steeply because a layer's whole expert set runs on the CPU.
Calibration (assumption: linear): 33.3 us per CPU-computed expert activation; 0.836 MiB per resident expert slot (mixE4K).
PREDICTED (not measured): at ~897 MiB, 16 slots/layer => 298-358 t/s serial (vs static 212), up to 517-704 if CPU misses overlap GPU hits; at ~736 MiB, 8 slots => 182-214 serial (vs static 161). Cold-start hit rates (conservative; warm caches higher).
Limits: logical trace, cold-start per phase; assumes miss cost linear and no PCIe transfers; Granite is not a stress model; the 1B/32-expert statistics must not be extrapolated to the target model (needs target traces).
Validation needed: a real hit/miss dispatch implementation (Strata-style) => delegated to focused harness (cc/hybrid_expert). Until then this is a hypothesis with a stated discriminating experiment.
=== decisions/D015-ssd-tier-emulation.md
# D015 — SSD-tier emulation via container memory limit (job-6e6b2d39b8; engine b0, mixE4K, --n-cpu-moe 24, own-file cold cache)
Class: MIXED. Transfers: the existence/shape of the page-cache cliff, I/O accounting method, cold-vs-warm discipline. Does NOT transfer: absolute t/s (discrete GPU, Zen2 CPU AVX2, PCIe, local NVMe, Linux page cache; target is unified memory with its own SSD).
Method: all expert weights file-backed in host memory (GPU holds attention+embeddings only: 572-576 MiB), `docker --memory L --memory-swap L`, posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) on the model file only (no host-wide flush), cgroup memory.peak and io.stat rbytes sampled at 4 Hz.
Result (pp512 / tg64, 3 reps; CONCURRENT COMPILE LOAD avg ~18 on 16 threads => speeds are lower bounds): limit -> tg t/s, SSD read: 1536m -> 129, 1.6 GiB; 1024m -> 79, 4.1 GiB; 768m -> 15, 28.8 GiB; 640m -> 3, 95.7 GiB; 560m -> 1, 135 GiB. All runs exit 0, no OOM kill.
Interpretation: working set ~ process anon (~400 MiB incl. CUDA/ggml buffers) + ~750 MiB expert bytes. Once the limit drops below it, decode becomes SSD-bound with heavy read amplification (reads >> useful bytes: 135 GiB for a run of a few hundred tokens). Advisor bound tokens/s <= effective SSD B/s / fetched B/token is consistent with the ~15 t/s point if nearly every expert is re-fetched each token (~160 MiB/token if all 192 activations miss).
Implication for the target: naive mmap + OS LRU has no notion of routing skew or layer order; an explicit hot-expert residency policy + prefetch/read-ahead control is the component to evaluate (trace-driven sizing in D014 gives the hit rate that policy needs).
Caveat to fix in a clean rerun: CPU contention; 1 repetition per limit; the 1536m row includes the initial model load reads.
=== decisions/D016-image-identity-confusion.md
# D016 — Build CC recorded the wrong "image config id" (found by independent observation, T-K)
Evidence: experiments/handoff-real/verdict.json (first rejection), cc/engine_handoff/example-real/{facts.json,verdict.json}, archive builds/results/b0-baseline-3/engine-image.docker.tar (index.json top digest sha256:cf383f82..., manifest.json Config sha256:7c2b92ad...).
Finding: with Docker 29's containerd image store, `docker image inspect .Id` returns the OCI INDEX digest (cf383f82...), not the image config digest (7c2b92ad...). The Build CC (written by Codex T-D from the brief's own warning) still stored the inspect Id as the image identity; `lab image-load --expect-config-id` therefore "verified" a value that is not a config id. The handoff tool refused to admit it because it re-observed the archive instead of trusting the record. It also showed the record hashed 7 of 19 executables in /app (libraries omitted).
Why it matters: the brief says to distinguish archive hash, Docker config ID, platform manifest digest and index digest; a lab that loads the archive needs the identity that the receiving engine can actually check.
Fix: Build CC now records image.docker_reported_id, image.config_digest, image.index_digest, image.index_manifests (parsed from the saved archive) and app_files (all regular files in /app), with a note; unit test asserts they are separate. Admission (lab image-load) to use archive-derived ids (next).
Lesson (methodology + Manager): identity checks must be performed by an independent observer on the delivered bytes; a record written by the producer is a claim. Two CCs written independently agreed on field names but not on meaning.
=== decisions/D017-routing-skew-control.md
# D017 — Is Granite routing skew real? (answering claim-register P12; ProMoE says modern MoEs have near-uniform expert access)
Evidence: experiments/routing/{control_uniform,prose,code,chat}.json (trace_replay), artifacts/traces/out/*.jsonl. Control = SYNTHETIC uniform-random top-8 trace (24 layers x 2000 decode tokens), labelled.
- Control hit rate (LRU and LFU) = slots/32 exactly (12.4, 24.9, 37.4, 49.9, 74.9%): simulator has no bias.
- Real Granite decode traces (cold start, 96-160 decode tokens, single sequence): LRU at 8 slots prose 49% / code 36% / chat 45% (LFU up to 49%) vs 25% control; at 16 slots 70-81% vs 50%; at 24 slots 88-94% vs 75%. => within-request skew/temporal locality is REAL for Granite.
- Mild: normalised usage entropy 0.88-0.92 (1.0 = uniform). Pooling the three workloads raises it to 0.936; top-8 hottest experts overlap 0.47 between workloads (random 0.25). => partially shared hot set, weaker when pooled; consistent in direction with MoE-Infinity (skew within request, weaker pooled) and ProMoE (near-uniform at scale).
Limits: 3 workloads, 1 sequence each, 96-160 decode tokens (cold-start dominated), prefill excluded from decode stats, Granite != target. Does NOT show the target model's routing is skewed. Needed before sizing any hot-expert cache: target-model traces across domains, long decodes, pooled multi-request.
Effect on D014: the prediction stands only as "if the target routes like Granite"; it must be re-derived from target traces. Claim P12 status: partially supported locally for Granite (within-request), pooled-uniformity question open.
=== decisions/D018-directive-strata-concepts-and-budget.md
# D018 — Directive (user, mid-session): apply Strata's concepts to Granite to reduce GPU memory; impose a memory restriction to simulate a super-big MoE
Answer to "have you applied Strata stuff?": not before this point (only studied, ran 4 CPU tests; used llama.cpp-native quantization and static --n-cpu-moe). Now:
1. Memory restriction = GPU budget shim (T-L, cc/gpu_budget): hard cap + virtual cudaMemGetInfo, scaled budget ~700 MiB (500GB->128GB ratio x 2.67GB), plus the container cgroup limit for the host/SSD tier (D015).
2. Strata concept -> Granite: expert residency table with hot experts in fast memory and cold in host memory, expert-granular placement. Proposed mechanism for llama.cpp: expert tensors in CUDA managed memory (each expert is one contiguous byte range of the ggml tensor: offset e*nb[2]); per-layer hot sets from routing traces get cudaMemAdvise(PreferredLocation=device)+prefetch; cold experts stay host-resident and are read by the same kernels (maps onto unified memory); static hot sets need no host sync and keep CUDA graphs. Dynamic LRU slots (Strata's hit_hook) are a later step. Delegated to an Opus agent (hard systems task).
Honesty: managed-memory behavior under oversubscription on this driver/GPU is unverified; PCIe remote reads are discrete-only cost; result classes will be labelled.
=== decisions/D019-hybrid-harness-result.md
# D019 — hybrid_moe_bench (Opus T-J) result on the D014 prediction (all timings UNSCORED/exploratory; discrete GPU; synthetic activations; replayed routing)
Evidence: cc/hybrid_expert/{RESULTS.md,results.json,results_L12_single_layer.json}, artifacts/opus-hybrid/, evidence/opus-hybrid.jsonl (ops op-eb0f9a7be446 build 350 s; op-2ea9dea3e2e5 24-layer run 62 s).
- Correctness: all-hit hybrid == GPU reference and zero-hit hybrid == CPU-all, bitwise, all 24 layers; mixed hit/miss within 1.5x the larger endpoint error vs fp64 (CPU quantizes activations Q8_K, CUDA Q8_1 => backends differ by float noise by construction).
- Miss cost: 30.6 us marginal per CPU-computed expert + ~15 us fixed per layer with any miss (DRAM-bound ~29 GB/s) -> confirms the 33.3 us calibration (D014). AVX2 Q4_K dot confirmed by disassembly.

tool_input.prompt:
External research survey. Write ONE file: /home/muk/projects/siminfeng/campaign/research/external-survey.md (≤ 200 lines). No edits elsewhere; no installs, builds, GPU, or downloads beyond reading web pages / GitHub READMEs / API JSON (curl or WebFetch/WebSearch if available; `git ls-remote` ok). Do not clone large repos. Today is 2026-11-10; prefer sources ≥2 weeks old for any version recommendation.

Our situation: a campaign improving MoE inference via llama.cpp (pinned 31288c9c6, Oct–Nov 2026) on two hosts: x86 Ryzen + RTX 5070 Ti (sm_120, CUDA 12.8, Docker/Buildx images) and Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB (sm_87, JetPack 6.2.3 / L4T R36.5.2, CUDA 12.6, host-native builds packaged on l4t-cuda:12.6.11-runtime). Goal: run MoE models several times larger than memory (unified memory + NVMe/SSD) at good quality and t/s. Findings: decode GPU-kernel bound; fused MoE gate/up kernels slow on Orin for bf16/Q4_K; llama.cpp `-lm auto` disables mmap on integrated GPUs; cgroup memory caps do not bound CUDA allocations on Tegra; nvidia-smi useless on Orin; ncu counters admin-only.

Survey, each item with: URL, what it is, version/date, license, platform support (aarch64/Jetson/sm_87? sm_120?), what we would use it for, verdict (adopt / study / watch / reject), and HOW YOU FOUND IT (search query, citation chain, README link, awesome-list) — this provenance is required.
A. Inference engines/forks with MoE offload/streaming: ik_llama.cpp, KTransformers, PowerInfer/PowerInfer-2, MoE-Infinity, Fiddler, llama.cpp upstream changes after 31288c9c6 touching MoE offload, `--moe-cache-mib`, iGPU/UMA mmap (issues #15034, #28160 referenced in source), CUDA graphs on MoE; MLC-LLM, TensorRT-LLM / TensorRT Edge-LLM for Jetson, vLLM on Jetson, SGLang. For llama.cpp upstream, use `git ls-remote https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp` and GitHub API/commit search to find relevant newer PRs (titles+numbers).
B. Jetson build/image tooling: dusty-nv jetson-containers (build system, l4t base images, version matrix), NVIDIA L4T container catalog (l4t-cuda, l4t-jetpack tags), JetPack 6.2/7 compatibility, NVIDIA container toolkit CSV mode on Tegra.
C. Profiling/observability on Jetson & desktop: Nsight Systems/Compute versions for L4T, jtop/jetson-stats, tegrastats alternatives, NVTX in llama.cpp, eBPF/bpftrace for page-fault/I/O tracing (availability on L4T kernels), blktrace, `perf` on Tegra, fio for NVMe baselines.
D. Labs/isolation/reproducibility: BuildKit reproducible builds (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, -ffile-prefix-map), Testcontainers, BenchExec, systemd-run scopes for cgroup isolation, how others cap GPU memory on Jetson (if any).
E. Recent papers (2024–2026) on MoE expert offloading / SSD streaming / unified memory (e.g. on Apple/Jetson/DGX Spark): give arXiv IDs, one-line mechanism, and whether code exists.
End with a ranked "Top 10 to act on" for us, and a short "How to keep finding sources" method (feeds, queries, citation-chasing). Reply ≤ 12 lines.

# D025 — Full-engine decode gain on Jetson: route bf16 MoE gate/up (batch 1) to MMF instead of fused MMVF (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
Claim category: **full-engine code gain (local to jetson-arm, sm_87, bf16 Granite-3.1-1b-a400m, batch-1 decode)**. Not transferred to x86 (untested there).
- Candidate: llama.cpp 31288c9c6 + cc/moe_dispatch_sm87/patches/combined-01-02.patch (sha256 9cd5745b…), env-gated, default = upstream. Image campaign/llamacpp:jetson-c1-j3 (Build CC record cc/build_engine/results/jetson-c1-j3/build-record.json, archive b730a81f…). Same image for all arms → only the env switch differs.
- Mechanism (J-T3 source analysis + independent review): the fused gate/up+GLU pattern asks the MMVF heuristic ("src0 rows ≤ 512" → vector kernel, 256 threads, F32 activations); standalone NVIDIA bf16 MUL_MAT_ID uses MMF (tensor-core MMA). `GGML_CUDA_J_MMF_IDS=1` declines that fusion on cc 870 when MMF is eligible. nsys (J-P002): gate/up per layer-token 385 µs fused MMVF → 2×131 µs MMF (+GLU kernel); kernel count +3120/64 tok (nothing skipped); GPU time −8.8% under tracing.
- Speed (J-E005, counterbalanced base,P1,P2,F,F,P2,P1,base; tg128 r5; steady = samples 2-5): base 50.48/50.20, **P1 60.07/60.05 (+19.3%)**, P2 (128-thread MMVF) 59.56/59.30 (+18.0%), all-fusion-off 57.34/57.33 (+13.9%). Depth 1024: base 48.7/48.6 → P1 57.8/57.8 (+19%). Prefill pp512 unchanged (1105–1149 both arms, base inert = same as unpatched image 50.4).
- Quality: batch-512 ppl20 identical (path not exercised there — prefill unaffected by design). Decode path (perplexity -ub 1, c128 x 8): base 8.0332, P1 8.0163, P2 8.0358. KL vs saved base logits: A/A mean ≈0 (max 6e-5 storage floor); **P1 mean KLD 2.7e-4, 99% 4.2e-3, max 9.1e-3, top-1 99.6%**; P2 2.0e-4, top-1 99.2%. For scale x86 Q8_0 vs bf16: 3.4e-3, 97.0% (D010). 64-token greedy text byte-identical for all arms.
- Precision note: MMF rounds F32 activations to bf16 before MMA (mmf.cuh:202-212) — a small numerics change, same class the down-projection already has in the base. Not "bit-exact"; passes the D005 smoke gate and a token-level check.
- Limits: one host, one model/precision, batch 1 decode, MAXN_SUPER with dynamic GPU devfreq (not pinned); only 2 runs per arm (each 5 reps) — effect (≈+10 t/s) ≫ A/A spread (≤0.3 t/s). Unknown on quantized weights (Q8_0/Q4 take MMVQ, different path), on multi-sequence decode, on other cc.
- Next discriminating experiment (x86): drop the `cc == 870` guard (or add cc 1200) and run the same A/B on the 5070 Ti — whether discrete Blackwell has the same MMVF-vs-MMF gap is unknown.

=== decisions/D028-cgroup-cap-not-cuda-boundary-tegra.md
# D028 — Container memory cap is NOT a reliable bound on CUDA allocations on Tegra (2026-11-10, jetson-arm)
- Probe: cc/smoke/cuda_alloc_probe.cu (cudaMalloc / cudaHostAlloc-mapped in 250 MiB chunks, each touched by a kernel), ubuntu:22.04 + nvidia runtime, `--memory 1g --memory-swap 1g`.
- Results (ops J-ISO1 in evidence/jetson-arm/opus-jetson.jsonl):
  - 2 runs (device, host-mapped): killed with exit 137 after 1000 / 750 MiB (first attempts after the D022 env fix).
  - control 600 MiB device: OK.
  - 5 later runs, 1500 MiB device under the same 1 GiB cap: ALL completed (exit 0, OOMKilled=false); container cgroup memory.current peaked at 629–638 MiB while 1500 MiB was allocated and touched; memory.events empty.
- Interpretation: cudaMalloc/nvmap pages on Orin are largely not charged to the allocating container's memory cgroup (only ~0.6 GiB, likely context/runtime/host-side buffers, is). The two early kills are unexplained (possibly charging of first-touch pages under conditions not reproduced) → the cap neither reliably limits nor reliably passes GPU allocations.
- Decision: never describe a Docker `--memory` limit as a GPU or shared-DRAM budget on Jetson (same rule as the campaign prompt for x86 VRAM). Budget field in admission must be `guarantee: none-for-device-allocations` on Tegra. Over-memory experiments use the PHYSICAL limit (20.8 GiB model on 7.4 GiB DRAM) + the J-OM1 watchdog for host safety; a cooperative cap (cc/gpu_budget cudaMemGetInfo/cudaMalloc interposer) is the remaining candidate for an artificial budget — unqualified on Jetson.
- Open: reproduce the early kills (order effects? page-cache charging of the bind-mounted binary? first container start?) — low priority.

# Paper Claim Register (upstream claims, NOT local facts)

Read date: 2026-11-09. Every claim below is what a paper says under ITS conditions. Nothing here has been tested on our proxy
(RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB + 48 GB RAM + NVMe, granite-3.1-1b-a400m, 24 layers x 32 experts, top-8, llama.cpp). Status of every claim: source-supported.

How read: arXiv abs page (version/date from listing) + PDF text extracted locally with pdftotext from the arXiv PDF of the stated version.
Section/figure numbers are taken from the extracted text; where I could not pin a number I say "location approximate".
Papers were read selectively (grep + targeted passages), not cover-to-cover.

Target = unified memory, ~500 GB weights -> 128 GB + 4 TB SSD, single/low-batch interactive decode.
Verdicts: reproduce | adapt mechanism | inspiration only | not applicable.

Key framing caveat: nearly all offloading papers below assume DISCRETE memory (PCIe is the bottleneck). On unified memory there is
no CPU->GPU copy; the tiers are RAM (high BW) and SSD (low BW). Latency numbers do not transfer; hit-rate / accuracy / predictability
properties (model properties) can transfer.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## P01 Fiddler - CPU compute vs weight transfer for missed experts
- Paper: Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of MoE Models, arXiv 2402.07033, read v3 (1 May 2025; ICLR 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07033
- Location: Sec 1 / Sec 3.1-3.3 (latency model, Algorithm 1), Appendix A + Fig 7 (microbenchmark), Sec 4.2 Fig 4 (result).
- Claim: Expert-layer CPU latency grows ~linearly with number of input tokens; GPU latency ~constant but needs weight transfer when expert not resident;
  transfer time "independent of the batch size". For small inputs it is faster to run a missed expert on the CPU than copy its weights. Activation copy is <1% of latency.
  Result: 1.26x avg speedup over best baseline (llama.cpp) in single-request end-to-end tok/s; 1.30x on long prefill (TTFT); 11.57x beam search (abstract numbers).
- Conditions: Mixtral-8x7B 16-bit (>90 GB); Env1 Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB + Xeon 6126 48c, PCIe3 x16 (32 GB/s), 56/256 experts on GPU; Env2 RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB + Xeon 8480+ 112c, PCIe4 (64 GB/s), 125/256 on GPU.
  ShareGPT, input 32-256, output 64-512, SINGLE request (batch 1; beam widths 4-16 for the 11.57x). Baselines DeepSpeed-MII, Mixtral-Offloading, llama.cpp b2956. 16-bit weights in host DRAM (no SSD).
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (unified memory has no transfer; "CPU vs GPU for a miss" becomes "compute from RAM vs stream from SSD", where SSD read-then-compute vs partial compute is a different tradeoff).
  Proxy = adapt mechanism (we can measure CPU-expert vs PCIe-copy crossover; granite experts are tiny).
- Hypothesis: For one decode token on granite, computing a non-resident expert on the CPU (from RAM) is faster than PCIe-copying it to the GPU and computing there, for all experts sizes in this model.
- Experiment: microbench per-expert CPU matvec (llama.cpp CPU backend, Q4_K) vs cudaMemcpy of one expert tensor slice + GPU matvec, token count 1,8,64. Refuted if copy+GPU <= CPU latency at 1 token.
  Transfer to unified target: ratio does NOT transfer (no copy); only the batch-dependence shape (CPU linear, GPU flat) is portable.
- Status: source-supported.

## P02 MoE-Infinity - skew is per-request, vanishes across requests (batch 1)
- Paper: MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache, arXiv 2401.14361, read v3 (12 Mar 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14361
- Location: Sec 1 Contribution 1; Sec 4 (Fig 2 expert reuse counts; text "Analyzing over 1000 sequences"); Table 2 / Fig 3-4 (K-means groups, Markov chain).
- Claim (quote): "With a batch size of one ... memory available on a consumer-grade GPU is often sufficient to store the most frequently used experts during decoding";
  "experts exhibit skewed reuse patterns when continuously decoding tokens within a single request... However, this reuse pattern is only present at the request level;
  after processing multiple requests, the skew disappears, and all experts tend to be activated uniformly." Hence global-frequency caching fails; per-request activation traces (EAMs) are needed.
- Conditions: DeepSeek-V2-Lite and others (Mixtral, Switch, NLLB, Arctic); traces from BigBench/FLAN/MMLU; batch size 1; no GPU/SSD numbers for this specific claim (analysis).
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (the property is model/workload-level, memory-tier independent; reuse within a request is exactly what a 128 GB cache + SSD needs). Proxy = reproduce on granite traces.
- Hypothesis: On our granite traces, per-request frequency (or recency) residency achieves a higher hit rate than a single global static top-k set chosen from pooled traces at equal budget (16/32), and the global distribution is closer to uniform than per-request.
- Experiment (offline, no GPU): replay existing routing traces; compute per-layer expert-usage entropy pooled vs per-request; hit rate of (a) global static top-16 (b) per-request LFU/LRU (c) random static (expected 50%). Refuted if (a) >= (b) within noise or pooled entropy ~ per-request entropy.
  Transfers to unified target: qualitatively yes IF the large model's routing resembles granite (fine-grained experts); magnitude is model specific.
- Status: source-supported.

## P03 MoE-Infinity - trace-guided cache+prefetch latency
- Paper: same as P02 (v3). Location: Table 1 (p1), Fig 7 (Sec 5.1), Fig 9 (EAMC capacity), Table 3 (workload shift).
- Claim: DeepSeek-V2-Lite TPOT (time per output token) on one A5000 24 GB: MoE-Infinity 155 ms vs vLLM 485, DeepSpeed 737, Mixtral-Offloading 1250, Ollama (llama.cpp) 2590 ms (avg TPOT) = 3.1x-16.7x.

## P04 FlexGen - SSD tier is viable only for throughput; latency-insensitive batched
- Paper: FlexGen: High-Throughput Generative Inference of LLMs with a Single GPU, arXiv 2303.06865, read v2 (12 Jun 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06865
- Location: Sec 1 bullets; Fig 1 (latency-throughput); Table 1 (hardware); Sec 6.1 Table 2; Appendix A.4 (Table 24 SSD speeds).
- Claim: OPT-175B on one 16 GB T4 reaches 1 tok/s with effective batch size 144 (4608 tokens generated) at ~4000 s block latency (4-bit, weights held in CPU RAM, no disk);
  without compression 69x over baselines at batch up to 256 / 12000 s latency. "The batch size of 1 did not result in a noticeably better latency" (Appx) - i.e. batch-1 latency is poor.
- Conditions: T4 16 GB, 208 GB DRAM, 1.5 TB cloud NVMe SSD (read ~2 GB/s), OPT-30B/175B, prompt 512, output 32, THROUGHPUT/batched, dense model, latency-insensitive.
  Authors state unified-memory architectures "could be more friendly to our approach" (Appx, no experiment).
- Applicability: target = not applicable for the throughput result (we need single-request tok/s). Inspiration only for the lesson: when weights spill to SSD, decode rate is bounded by SSD BW / bytes touched per token unless batch amortizes. Proxy = inspiration only.
- Hypothesis: In the SSD-bound regime, single-request decode tok/s is approximately SSD_BW / (bytes of non-resident experts touched per token), within 30%.
- Experiment: container memory-limit run (known collapse regime) logging read bytes/token via iostat/perf vs measured tok/s; fio sequential and 4k-random expert-sized read BW. Refuted if model error >30% (page-cache readahead/granularity dominates).

- Status: source-supported.

## P05 FlexGen - 4-bit group-wise quantization of weights+KV to avoid disk
- Paper: same as P04 (v2). Location: Sec 5 (group-wise quantization), Table 5 (accuracy), Sec 6.1 (effective batch 144 + compression fits CPU memory).
- Claim: Group-wise 4-bit weights and KV cache, no retraining/calibration: OPT-175B Lambada acc 0.758 (FP16) -> 0.756 (4-bit); WikiText ppl 10.82 -> 10.94; OPT-30B ppl 12.72 -> 12.90.
  Compression's throughput benefit comes mainly from fitting in CPU memory and avoiding SSD swapping (112x vs baselines with compression at prompt 512).

- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (reducing bytes moved is the lever when below working-set RAM). Proxy = reproduce the principle (we already measured Q4 vs mixed precision quality; the untested part is tok/s vs bytes under SSD/page-cache pressure).
- Hypothesis: At fixed (insufficient) RAM, decode tok/s scales with 1/(expert bytes): Q4 experts give >=1.5x tok/s over Q8 experts in the page-cache-collapse regime.
- Experiment: same container limit, run Q8 vs Q4 vs Q3 expert GGUFs, record tok/s and read MB/token. Refuted if speedup <1.3x or does not track bytes ratio.

- Status: source-supported.

## P06 PowerInfer - hot/cold split from power-law activation
- Paper: PowerInfer: Fast LLM Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU, arXiv 2312.12456, read v2 (12 Dec 2024; SOSP 2024). https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12456
- Location: Sec 3.1 Insight-1 / Fig 4 (CDF), footnote 3; Table 1 (sparsity); Sec 8.2, Fig 10 / Fig 14 (batch scaling).
- Claim: Neuron activation follows a power law: a minority of "hot" neurons carries ~80% of activations (OPT-30B ~26% of neurons; LLaMA2-70B ReGLU ~43%; SwiGLU-70B ~69% per Sec 3.1 and footnote 3; figures partially garbled in extraction, check Fig 4 before citing).
  Preloading hot neurons on GPU and computing cold on CPU: avg 8.32 tok/s, up to 16.06 tok/s, up to 11.69x over llama.cpp on RTX 4090 (24 GB); GPU handles ~70% of neuron load (vs 20% llama.cpp). Speedup shrinks as batch grows (Fig 14); input-heavy/short-output cases only 1.07x-4x.
- Conditions: ReLU-family sparse models (OPT, Falcon-ReLU-40B, ReGLU LLaMA2-70B); RTX 4090 24GB (PC-High) and 2080Ti 11GB (PC-Low); batch size 1 default; Alpaca/ChatGPT prompts 8-128 tokens; FP16 and INT4; trained activation predictors; best gains need high-sparsity ReLU models.
- Applicability: target = inspiration only (neuron-level sparsity of dense models, not expert routing; SwiGLU models gain much less). Proxy = inspiration only; the analog is expert-level skew (see P12 which suggests modern fine-grained MoEs are flatter).
- Hypothesis: The top 25% of granite experts per layer account for >50% of routed token-expert assignments in our traces (i.e. a real power law exists at expert granularity).
- Experiment: compute per-layer expert usage CDF from existing traces (also per domain). Refuted if top-8/32 experts cover <40% (near-uniform = 25%).
  Transfer: skew property is model-specific; the target model's own router stats must be measured.
- Status: source-supported.

## P07 vLLM / PagedAttention - KV cache fragmentation
- Paper: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention, arXiv 2309.06180, read v1 (12 Sep 2023; SOSP 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180
- Location: Sec 3 / Fig 2 ("only 20.4%-38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store actual token states" in existing systems); Sec 6 Fig 12-14 (throughput).
- Claim: Existing systems waste 62-80% of KV memory through reservation/fragmentation; PagedAttention (block-table paging) gets near-zero waste, enabling larger batches: 2-4x throughput at same latency vs FasterTransformer/Orca (more at longer sequences, larger models, complex sampling).
- Conditions: A100 40GB (OPT-13B), 4xA100 (66B), 8xA100-80GB (175B); ShareGPT/Alpaca; many concurrent requests (batch-serving throughput); dense OPT/LLaMA.
- Applicability: target = not applicable for the 2-4x (we are single-request, no KV fragmentation problem). Inspiration only for the paging abstraction and for budgeting: KV competes with experts for fast memory (see P03 Fig 8). Proxy = not applicable.
- Hypothesis: At our intended context lengths, KV cache for the target model is <10% of the 128 GB budget, so KV management is not a first-order lever.
- Experiment: compute KV bytes = 2*layers*kv_heads*head_dim*ctx*bytes for target config (needs target model config - unknown to me) and measure granite KV size/tok/s vs ctx 2k/8k/32k. Refuted if KV >10% at the target context.
  Transfer: arithmetic transfers once target config is known; granite measurement does not.
- Status: source-supported.

## P08 MxMoE - bits by block sensitivity x expert frequency; linear-block granularity
- Paper: MxMoE: Mixed-precision Quantization for MoE with Accuracy and Performance Co-Design, arXiv 2505.05799, read v1 (9 May 2025; ICML 2025 format). https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05799
- Location: Sec 3.1 + Fig 1a/1b (sensitivity and activation-frequency heterogeneity, DeepSeekV2-Lite layer 11); Sec 5.4 Table 3 (granularity); Sec 4.2 Eq 7 (ILP).
- Claim: Sensitivity varies across experts and across linear blocks inside an expert (e.g. Down proj of Expert 40 needs more bits than Gate proj); expert activation frequencies within one MoE block vary by >10x (Fig 1b).
  Allocating bitwidth per linear block beats per-expert allocation at 5-bit w-a: DeepSeek-V2-Lite PPL 6.11 vs 6.32, avg acc 69.01 vs 67.88; Qwen1.5-MoE PPL 6.95 vs 6.98 (Table 3; the gain is small on some models).
- Conditions: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (29.3 GB), Qwen1.5-MoE (26.7), Qwen2-MoE (106.9), Mixtral-8x7B (92.9); RTX 4090; calibration-based sensitivity statistics; WikiText2 PPL + 7 zero-shot tasks (not KLD, no long-form generation); GPU-resident kernels (no offload).
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism (accuracy-per-byte allocation is hardware independent; frequency-weighting also tells which experts deserve precision vs residency). Proxy = adapt (stock llama.cpp quantizes per-tensor and each layer's experts are one 3D tensor, so per-expert precision is not available without a custom quantizer; per-layer and per-matrix-type (gate/up/down) precision IS available).
- Hypothesis: At equal total bytes, giving ffn_down (and/or high-frequency layers) more bits than gate/up lowers KLD vs uniform Q4 on granite.
- Experiment: llama-quantize with tensor-type overrides (down at Q6/Q5, gate/up at Q3/Q4, matched bytes) vs uniform Q4_K_M and our 4/8 mix; measure KLD vs bf16. Refuted if KLD not lower than the existing mixed result (0.040) at equal GB.
  Transfer: accuracy conclusions likely transfer to larger MoEs only partly (sensitivity patterns are model-specific); speed claims (kernel) do not.
- Status: source-supported.

## P09 MxMoE - very low bit (2.25-bit) MoE accuracy vs GPTQ
- Paper: same as P08 (v1). Location: Sec 5.2 Table 1; abstract.
- Claim: At 2.25 average bits (weight-only, group 128 asym + Hadamard): WikiText2 PPL MxMoE vs GPTQ*: DeepSeekV2-Lite 7.01 vs 8.49 (fp16 5.92); Qwen1.5-MoE 8.79 vs 11.19 (fp16 6.79; gap 2.40 = the abstract's "2.4 lower"); Qwen2-MoE 7.57 vs 7.98 (fp16 5.84); Mixtral 5.63 vs 5.69 (fp16 3.88).
  At 3.25-bit: MxMoE better than GPTQ except Qwen2-MoE (6.18 vs 6.11). Abstract also: up to 3.4x speedup over FP16 and up to 29.4% over uniform quant at equal accuracy (5-bit w-a; kernel throughput, Fig 5).
- Conditions: GPU-resident, RTX 4090, PPL gap numbers are for weight-only; the 3.4x and 29.4% are batched MoE-block kernel throughput (512 tokens memory-bound; 8192 compute-bound), not end-to-end single-token decode.
- Applicability: target = adapt mechanism for depth: indicates ~2-3 bit experts are feasible with allocation but degrade (PPL +1.7 to +2.0 on DeepSeek-Lite even with best method). Proxy = adapt (llama.cpp IQ2/IQ3 + imatrix is the closest available).
- Hypothesis: On granite, expert tensors at IQ3_XXS/IQ2_S with imatrix and Q8 attention remain within KLD ~2x of the Q4 mixed configuration while cutting expert bytes by 25-40%.
- Experiment: quantize expert tensors at Q3_K/IQ3/IQ2 with imatrix, keep attention Q8; measure KLD and size. Refuted if KLD >4x the Q4-mixed result at <=30% byte saving.
